set.statement: In randomized trials of people with chronic pain, mostly neuropathic or cancer pain (28 trials, 2,454 participants; 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small reduction in pain. Nabiximols (a THC and CBD spray used in the mouth) was the commonest product (13 of the 28 trials) and nearly all of the pooled trials tested it. In a 2015 meta-analysis of the parallel-group trials (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 37% of people on cannabinoids and 31% on placebo had their pain reduced by at least 30% (254 of 685 against 215 of 685, the crude totals of the 8 trials in the review's forest plot; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 7 of them of nabiximols and 1 of smoked THC, 1,370 people; I2 48%) that does not exclude no difference; the 7 nabiximols trials alone gave 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), and the one smoked-THC trial, of 50 people, the largest effect (OR 3.43, 1.03 to 11.48). Pain on a 0 to 10 scale was 0.46 points lower with nabiximols (95% CI 0.11 to 0.80 lower; 6 trials, 948 people; I2 59%); the review team rated both outcomes moderate certainty and names no threshold for a clinically important change. More people rated themselves improved overall (OR 2.08, 1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 people; low certainty by the review team), neuropathic-pain scale scores were 3.89 points lower on a 0 to 100 scale (0.47 to 7.32 lower), and the Brief Pain Inventory (-0.17, -0.50 to 0.16) and quality of life (EQ-5D, -0.01, -0.05 to 0.02) did not differ. The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain, which its Discussion narrows to neuropathic or cancer pain treated with smoked THC or nabiximols, but the outcomes so rated are either not statistically significant or small. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with long-lasting pain who took a cannabis medicine (in the combined trials, nearly always a THC and CBD mouth spray) scored their pain about half a point lower on a 0 to 10 scale than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo). About 37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%, a difference that could be due to chance. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
set.population: People with chronic pain (mostly neuropathic pain; also cancer pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, HIV neuropathy and others) in randomized trials published up to April 2015; ages are not reported in the review's main text
set.exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials: nabiximols (oromucosal THC and CBD spray) in 13 of the 28 trials and in nearly all pooled ones, also smoked THC, nabilone, THC spray, dronabinol, vaporized cannabis and others; doses are study conditions
set.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, parallel-group trials, random effects, cannabinoid against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% (254/685 vs 215/685, crude totals in the review's Figure 2; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 1,370 patients; I2 48%; GRADE moderate by the review team); the 7 nabiximols trials alone OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86); smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48; 50 patients); in Figure 2, 5 of the 8 trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly) and 3 favour placebo (none significantly); neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03; 6 trials); nabiximols: 0 to 10 pain scale WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11; 6 trials, 948 patients; I2 59%; moderate); Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16; 3 trials); Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47; 5 trials); global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 patients; I2 68%; low); EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02; 3 trials).
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: I2 48% and 59%: moderate heterogeneity. In the responder pool 5 of the 8 trials point towards benefit and 3 towards placebo, none of those 3 significantly (Figure 2), and the review says the continuous results were not consistent across trials; not rated down, because the intervals overlap and the pooled estimates point the same way, but a stricter reading could rate down here.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: low. The review team rated these outcomes moderate; the editors also rate down for imprecision, because the outcome that matters most to patients (at least 30% less pain) does not exclude no effect, and the pain-scale reduction, though precise, is small. The largest responder effect comes from the one smoked-THC trial of 50 people; the 7 nabiximols trials alone give OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86). Status replicated: 5 of the 8 responder trials point the same way (3 significantly), with moderate heterogeneity and 3 trials pointing towards placebo without significance (Figure 2, viewed at adjudication); the pain-scale pool has 6 trials whose individual results the article does not show.

set.statement: In randomized trials of people with multiple sclerosis (11 trials, 2,138 participants; 3 further trials in paraplegia, 142 participants, could not be pooled; of all 14 trials, 7 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, most often nabiximols (6 of the 14 trials and 4 of the 5 in the Ashworth pool), in trials whose follow-up, where printed, was 3 to 15 weeks, are associated with a small improvement in spasticity as patients rate it, but not detectably as clinicians measure it. In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), patients' own spasticity ratings (numerical rating or visual analogue scales) were 0.76 points lower (95% CI 0.14 to 1.38 lower; 3 trials, 698 people; I2 73%; low certainty by the review team) and more patients rated themselves improved overall (OR 1.44, 1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 people; low), while the Ashworth scale, a clinician's rating of muscle tone, did not clearly change (-0.12, -0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials; I2 0%; moderate; the overall value as corrected by the journal in 2015), nor did the share of people whose rated spasticity fell by at least 30% (OR 1.64, 0.95 to 2.83) or 50% (1.40, 0.81 to 2.41; 2 trials each), activities of daily living (Barthel index: the review prints three separate product estimates and no pooled one, all with intervals that include no difference) or walking speed (-0.86, -3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials). The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for spasticity, but none of the outcomes it rated moderate (Ashworth, Barthel index, walking speed) showed a clear difference. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with MS who took a cannabis medicine, most often a THC and CBD mouth spray, rated their muscle stiffness a little lower (0.76 points on the rating scales used) than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo), and more of them felt better overall. When doctors measured stiffness, there was no clear difference. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
set.exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials, most often nabiximols (also THC/CBD capsules, dronabinol and nabilone); doses are study conditions
set.outcome: Spasticity on the Ashworth scale (clinician-rated) and on patient-rated numerical rating or visual analogue scales; 30% and 50% reductions; patients' global impression of change; activities of daily living (Barthel index); walking speed
set.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, multiple sclerosis trials, random effects, against placebo: patient-rated spasticity (numerical rating or visual analogue scales) WMD -0.76 (95% CI -1.38 to -0.14; 3 trials, 698 patients; I2 73%; GRADE low by the review team); global impression of change OR 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94; 3 trials, 461 patients; low); Ashworth WMD -0.12 (-0.24 to 0.01; 5 trials; I2 0%; moderate; the overall as corrected in the abstract in July 2015, also printed in the text and Figure 3; Table 2 gives 1,244 patients, Figure 3's totals 590 and 544; Table 2's three values for this row are per-product estimates, nabiximols -0.11, -0.23 to 0.02, from 4 trials); 30% reduction OR 1.64 (0.95 to 2.83) and 50% reduction OR 1.40 (0.81 to 2.41), 2 trials each (low); Barthel index: three estimates printed beside nabilone (2 trials), dronabinol and THC/CBD, -0.58 (-1.73 to 0.56), 0.23 (-0.13 to 0.59) and -0.03 (-0.39 to 0.33), no pooled estimate (moderate); walking speed -0.86 (-3.08 to 1.36; 2 trials; moderate).
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The patient-rated difference excludes no effect (698 people) and the Ashworth interval is narrow; the responder analyses, 2 trials each, are imprecise but secondary; the Barthel index has no pooled estimate.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias and one for inconsistency: low, the review team's own rating for the patient-rated outcome. The clinician-rated null (Ashworth, moderate by the review team) fits a small effect that patients notice and the clinicians' scale misses, or patient ratings swayed by knowing the treatment; the trials cannot separate these. Status replicated: the review says studies generally suggested improvement, and the patient-rated and global-impression pools (3 trials each) point the same way; in the Ashworth forest plot (Figure 3, viewed at adjudication) the trial estimates lie on both sides of zero, none significant, and one three-arm trial (Zajicek 2003) enters twice against the same placebo group, with negligible weight.

set.statement: In randomized trials of people receiving chemotherapy (28 trials, 1,772 participants, mostly of nabilone, THC, levonantradol or dronabinol; 23 at high and 5 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo are associated with more people having complete control of nausea and vomiting: in a 2015 meta-analysis of the three placebo-controlled parallel-group trials that could be pooled (dronabinol or nabiximols; Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 47% on cannabinoids against 20% on placebo had a complete response (percentages given only in the abstract, their derivation not described; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 102 patients; I2 0%; low certainty by the review team). Twenty trials compared cannabinoids only with other anti-sickness medicines, most often prochlorperazine (13 of the 20, editors' count from the review's Table 1; 15 trials in all had a prochlorperazine arm). The review says, without pooled figures, that all the trials pointed towards more benefit with cannabinoids than with the other medicines or placebo, though not significantly in all; because these comparisons are not pooled, how cannabinoids compare with those medicines, or with the anti-sickness medicines in use today, is not shown here. A narrative review calls THC an effective treatment for nausea and vomiting with chemotherapy, citing one source, and says, without a cited source, that patients often find marijuana more effective (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In three small trials (102 people having chemotherapy), about 47 in 100 people who took a cannabis medicine (dronabinol or a THC and CBD spray) had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 who took a dummy medicine (placebo). Most of the other trials compared cannabis medicines with other anti-sickness medicines; the review says these leaned towards the cannabis medicines too, but it did not combine them and not every result was clear. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
set.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (dronabinol or nabiximols) against placebo, parallel-group trials, random effects: complete response 47% vs 20% (given only in the abstract; about 27 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 3.82 (95% CI 1.55 to 9.42; 3 trials, 102 patients; I2 0%; GRADE low by the review team). Comparisons with active anti-sickness medicines (20 trials; prochlorperazine in 13 of them, editors' count from Table 1) not pooled in the article; the review says all trials favoured cannabinoids, not significantly in all.

set.statement: For sleep problems, appetite and weight in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo or other treatments are too few, small or short to show whether they help: in a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), each of these conditions had one to four trials designed for it (four for appetite in HIV, at most two for each of the others) and none for depression, most of them small and many at high risk of bias. Sleep: in 19 placebo-controlled trials for chronic pain or multiple sclerosis, mainly of nabiximols, sleep-quality scores on 0 to 10 scales differed from placebo by -0.58 points in favour of cannabinoids (95% CI -0.87 to -0.29; 8 trials) and sleep-disturbance scores by -0.26, also in their favour (-0.52 to 0.00; 3 trials), both very low certainty by the review team; of two trials in sleep problems (54 participants), one in sleep apnoea (22 patients; attributed to nabilone in the review, although its reference list points to a dronabinol trial) reported a lower apnoea–hypopnoea index (-19.64, P = .02), and a crossover trial in fibromyalgia found nabilone better than amitriptyline for insomnia (-3.25, -5.26 to -1.24), in the wording the journal corrected in 2016; the review concludes, on low-quality evidence, that cannabinoids may improve sleep. Appetite in HIV: weight gain of 2 kg or more within 6 weeks with dronabinol against placebo, OR 2.2 (0.68 to 7.27; 1 trial, 88 patients), among 4 trials all at high risk of bias. Anxiety: one trial of cannabidiol in 24 people with generalized social anxiety disorder, measured during a simulated public-speaking test with 107 minutes of follow-up (anxiety factor -16.52, P = .01; very low). Depression: in 5 trials for other conditions, 3 found no difference and one found worse depression scores at the highest nabiximols dose (2.50, 0.38 to 4.62) but not at the two lower doses (very low). Psychosis: two trials of cannabidiol (71 participants) found no difference, with intervals too wide to show the absence of an effect (against amisulpride, BPRS -0.10, -9.20 to 8.90; 35 patients). Glaucoma: one crossover trial of 6 people found no difference in eye pressure. Tourette syndrome: two small trials of THC capsules (36 participants) suggested less tic severity on some scales (17 or 18 patients per analysis; low). Epilepsy was not among the review's conditions, and trials of cannabidiol medicines in epilepsy were not among the sources read for this claim; as human evidence a narrative review describes only a small parent survey of cannabidiol-rich cannabis in childhood epilepsy, in which, of 19 families, 2 reported freedom from seizures, 8 a fall in seizures of more than 80% and 6 a fall of 25 to 60%, and it calls safety and efficacy data on cannabis plant products for epilepsy insufficient (Volkow et al., 2014; second-hand). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: For sleep problems, appetite in HIV, anxiety, depression, psychosis, glaucoma and Tourette syndrome, there are only a few small, short trials of cannabis medicines each, so it is not known whether they help. Sleep scores in trials for pain or MS were slightly better with the medicine than with a dummy medicine (placebo), but this evidence is very weak. Epilepsy was not part of this review, and trials of a CBD medicine for epilepsy were not read for this answer.

set.statement: In randomized trials of cannabinoid medicines for many conditions (62 trials reported adverse events; parallel-group and crossover trials combined), cannabinoids at the highest dose each trial tested, compared with placebo or another medicine, increase short-term side effects (the review's authors word this as an association). Side effects were common in both groups: across the 29 trials with counts for any adverse event in the review's forest plot, 1,438 of 1,779 people on cannabinoids (about 81 in 100) and 1,058 of 1,710 on placebo or another medicine (about 62 in 100) had at least one (crude totals, editors' arithmetic; the review's table gives 3,714 patients for these trials). In a 2015 meta-analysis (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), the odds of any adverse event were 3.03 times higher (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%), of a serious adverse event 1.41 times (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%) and of leaving a trial because of adverse events 2.94 times (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients), with no difference in deaths (1.01, 0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients). Specific effects more frequent with cannabinoids included disorientation (OR 5.41, 2.61 to 11.19), dizziness (5.09, 4.10 to 6.32; 41 studies), euphoria (4.08, 2.18 to 7.64), confusion (4.03, 2.05 to 7.97), drowsiness (3.68, 2.24 to 6.01), dry mouth (3.50, 2.58 to 4.75), somnolence (2.83, 2.05 to 3.91), loss of balance (2.62, 1.12 to 6.13), hallucination (2.19, 1.02 to 4.68; 10 studies), nausea (2.08, 1.63 to 2.65), asthenia (2.03, 1.35 to 3.06), fatigue (2.00, 1.54 to 2.62), vomiting (1.67, 1.13 to 2.47) and diarrhoea (1.65, 1.04 to 2.62); depression, anxiety, paranoia, psychosis and seizures did not differ clearly, with wide intervals (psychosis 1.09, 0.07 to 16.35; 2 studies, 37 patients). Apart from the counts for any adverse event, the review reports odds ratios only, not how many people in 100 had each effect; using the highest dose was the authors' choice of a worst case; and no study of long-term adverse events was found, even among non-randomized studies. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In short trials, side effects were common with both cannabis medicines and the comparison: about 81 in 100 people taking a cannabis medicine and 62 in 100 taking a dummy medicine (placebo) or another medicine had at least one. Cannabis medicines raised the odds of any side effect, and of stopping the trial because of one, about three times, and of a serious one 1.4 times. Disorientation, dizziness, feeling high, confusion, drowsiness and dry mouth were among the most increased; nausea and vomiting were also more common. Deaths did not differ. The review used the highest dose each trial gave, gave counts only for having any side effect, and found no studies of long-term harms.
set.magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, cannabinoid (highest dose) against placebo or active comparator, all indications, parallel-group and crossover trials: any adverse event, crude totals in Figure 4 1,438/1,779 vs 1,058/1,710 (80.8% vs 61.9%, editors' arithmetic; 3,489 patients against 3,714 in Table 3), OR 3.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 3.80; 29 studies, 3,714 patients; I2 31%); serious 1.41 (1.04 to 1.92; 34 studies, 3,248 patients; I2 0%); withdrawal due to adverse events 2.94 (2.18 to 3.96; 23 studies, 2,755 patients); death 1.01 (0.51 to 2.00; 5 studies, 929 patients); psychiatric disorders 3.10 (1.81 to 5.29; 8 studies); nervous system disorders 3.17 (2.20 to 4.58; 10 studies). set.grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias: moderate for the short-term excess of adverse events as worded. The causal verb is the editors', used because the evidence is randomized and the certainty moderate; the review's authors word it as an association, and the review itself gives no GRADE rating for adverse events. Odds ratios overstate relative risks for common events: for any adverse event the crude totals are about 81 against 62 in 100, a ratio of about 1.3 (editors' arithmetic), against a pooled odds ratio of 3.03; no absolute frequencies are reported for individual events. Status replicated: 23 to 41 studies per main estimate, with low heterogeneity.

set.statement: In studies of pregnant women and their newborns published from 1982 to 2014 (24 articles from 19 studies, mostly cohorts; 15 of the 24 articles before 2000, editors' count; English only), any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (women using other illicit drugs left out, but not those who smoked tobacco or drank alcohol), compared with no cannabis use during pregnancy, is associated with somewhat smaller babies and more admissions to intensive care; whether it is linked to early birth is uncertain. In a 2016 meta-analysis whose pooled estimates are not stated to be adjusted for anything (the mean differences were pooled from raw group means, so they are unadjusted; Gunn et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low), exposed babies weighed on average about 109 g less at birth (95% CI 39 to 180 g; 10 studies, 4 of them finding lower weight; I2 63%), and had higher odds of weighing under 2,500 g (OR 1.77, 1.04 to 3.01; 7 studies, 2 of them positive; I2 89%) and of admission to neonatal or other intensive care (OR 2.02, 1.27 to 3.21; 4 studies, 3 positive; I2 78%); the estimate for preterm birth (before 37 weeks in most studies) fits both no difference and about twice the odds (OR 1.29, 0.80 to 2.08; 9 studies), and length of pregnancy, length and head size at birth, Apgar scores, birth defects and deaths around the time of birth showed no clear difference. No absolute risks were reported in the article, and the review does not discuss whether intensive-care admission reflects the babies' health or hospital practice toward babies of mothers known to use drugs (editors' observation). Mothers who used cannabis also had higher odds of anaemia (OR 1.36, 1.10 to 1.69; 6 studies), a result carried mainly by one large study. The review's authors say that, because most studies did not separate cannabis from tobacco and alcohol, and tobacco and heavy alcohol use are established causes of low birth weight, preterm birth and babies small for their gestational age, they cannot tell whether the associations come from cannabis. As described second-hand in narrative reviews and a professional statement: an earlier meta-analysis linked regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy with lower birth weight, a smaller reduction than with tobacco smoking, and one large study found no rise in birth defects (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009); later large studies reported that the lower birth weight generally persisted after statistical control for other drug use, although cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully, and self-reported use under-counts use, which Hall says probably weakens the associations (Hall, 2015); and in one US state with legal cannabis, prenatal use went with 1.5 times the odds of low birth weight after adjustment for maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use (OR 1.5, 1.1 to 2.1; Crume et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.plain: In studies mostly from before 2000, babies of women who used cannabis in pregnancy weighed on average about 109 grams less at birth than babies of women who did not, and more often went to newborn intensive care. Whether they were more often born early is not clear, and birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common. Many of the mothers also smoked tobacco or drank alcohol; smoking and heavy drinking can also make babies smaller, and most studies did not separate them from cannabis, so the studies cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.
set.exposure: Any cannabis use during pregnancy as each study defined it (the authors note reliance on self-report, which may under-count use), with use of other illicit drugs excluded but tobacco and alcohol use allowed; frequency, amount, timing and potency not analysed
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Pooled estimates not stated to be adjusted for anything (continuous outcomes pooled from raw means and SDs, so unadjusted; whether any odds ratio taken from a paper was adjusted is not said), in which tobacco and alcohol use, both known causes of low birth weight and early birth, are not separated from cannabis; exposure largely self-reported and under-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gunn_2016). A stricter reading would rate down two levels; the floor is reached either way.
set.grade.domains.large_effect.note: The intensive-care odds ratio (2.02) is not stated to be adjusted and is open to confounding by tobacco and alcohol; no upgrade.

set.statement: As described in an American Heart Association scientific statement and in narrative reviews (all figures second-hand; no primary study was read here, and the statement gives no search or appraisal method), studies of adults who use cannabis point in different directions on heart attack, stroke and other heart and blood-vessel disease, and the AHA writing group judged the evidence still inconclusive (Page et al., 2020). In the hour after use, the risk of a heart attack starting was 4.8 times that at other times in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, an estimate printed without an interval that rests on few exposed people (9 had smoked cannabis within an hour of presenting with the heart attack, by the statement's account) (Mittleman et al., 2001, as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015, calls it a quadrupling). Two surveys found more stroke: past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 2.3 (95% CI 1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related factors including tobacco smoking, with the excess confined to weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7; adjustment not stated) (Hemachandra et al., 2016); and among adults aged 18 to 44, use went with an adjusted OR for stroke of 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al., 2020; adjustment set not stated). Health-record and hospital databases report more heart attacks where cannabis use is recorded, for example 1.37% against 0.54% over 3 years (about 14 against 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion; RR 2.53, adjustment not stated; Chami & Kim, 2019), but the statement warns that samples of hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias. Against these, in the CARDIA cohort (5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed for more than 25 years) cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., 2017; no estimates printed). After a heart attack the findings run both ways: long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; adjustment not stated; Frost et al., 2013), while among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, all-cause and cardiovascular mortality were higher (adjusted HR 1.99 and 2.22; no intervals printed) in people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it, which does not isolate cannabis (DeFilippis et al., 2018). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate, to which healthy young adults quickly become tolerant, and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; the angina finding also in Page et al., 2020). The statement names short-term, observational and retrospective designs, poorly measured exposure, recall bias, low-risk cohorts and confounding by tobacco as the main weaknesses, and judges the evidence for people with cardiac risk factors insufficient; Hall (2015) concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.magnitude: All second-hand. Case-crossover (Mittleman et al. 2001, 3,882 people with a heart attack): onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval; 9 people had smoked cannabis within 1 hour of presentation); follow-up of 1,913: mortality over 3.8 years 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Stroke: Hemachandra et al. 2016, past-year use, rate ratio 3.3 (1.8 to 6.3) before and 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1 to 10.7) for weekly or more frequent use; Parekh et al. 2020, adults aged 18 to 44, adjusted OR 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) for use on more than 10 days a month, and, for that frequent use together with combustible-cigarette use, 3.12 (1.40 to 6.97), and with e-cigarette use, 2.63 (1.07 to 6.46), each against people who did not use cannabis. Databases: Chami & Kim 2019, 3-year heart-attack incidence 1.37% vs 0.54% (about 14 vs 5 in 1,000, editors' conversion), RR 2.53 (2.45 to 2.61); Desai et al. 2019, heart-attack admissions of young adults 0.23% vs 0.14%. CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017, 5,113 adults, over 25 years): no association, no estimates printed. After a heart attack: Frost et al. 2013, mortality 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81 to 2.05, P = 0.28; DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults, adjusted HR 1.99 (all-cause) and 2.22 (cardiovascular) among people who used cocaine and marijuana, no intervals; Johnson-Sasso et al. 2018, mortality OR 0.79 (short-term outcomes by the reference title; no interval or adjustment printed). Laboratory: exercise time to angina 48% shorter after one cannabis cigarette than after placebo.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: The trigger estimate rests on few exposed people (9 had used within an hour of presentation, by the statement's account) and has no interval; stroke intervals are wide (2.1 to 10.7; 1.08 to 3.10); the CARDIA null is printed without estimates, so its precision is unknown; the mortality hazard ratios after a heart attack have no intervals.
set.grade.domains.large_effect.note: The 4.8-fold trigger estimate rests on few exposed people, without an interval or adjustment; no upgrade.
set.grade.domains.dose_response.note: Gradients by frequency (mortality after a heart attack; stroke with weekly or more frequent use) come second-hand from single studies without stated adjustment, and the AHA statement says many of the mortality findings did not reach statistical significance; no upgrade.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence seen only through reviews starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low, the floor. Overlapping sources are counted once: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and the AHA statement relay the same case-crossover study, and its mortality follow-ups (the 1,913-person study and Frost et al., 2013) come from the same onset study, so the trigger, the mortality gradient and the non-significant long-term mortality are not independent; the statement's inpatient analyses largely share one database. Contested because credible designs disagree (the long cohort against the trigger, survey and database studies; after a heart attack, a non-significant excess, a lower short-term mortality and a higher mortality in people who used cocaine and marijuana) and the reviews read the same evidence differently (still inconclusive for the AHA; probable for middle-aged adults in Hall, 2015). The claim rests only on second-hand sources (a professional statement without a stated search, and narrative reviews), so it stays at draft and says so (METHODS §6.3).
set.debate.evidence_yes: In a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack, the risk of onset in the 60 minutes after cannabis use was 4.8 times baseline; 37 had smoked cannabis within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation (Mittleman et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020, and Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), and in a follow-up of 1,913 of them mortality over 3.8 years rose with frequency of use, 2.5 times with use less than weekly and 4.2 times with use more than weekly (as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, without intervals; the AHA statement says many mortality findings of these smaller follow-up studies did not reach statistical significance). Among 2,097 young adults treated for a heart attack at two academic hospitals, adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause and cardiovascular death were 1.99 and 2.22 among people who used cocaine and marijuana, as the statement's table words it (DeFilippis et al., 2018, as relayed by Page et al., 2020). In a population survey, past-year use went with 3.3 times the rate of stroke or transient ischaemic attack and a rate ratio of 2.3 (1.1 to 4.5) after adjustment that included tobacco, the excess lying in weekly or more frequent use (4.7, 2.1 to 10.7); in a US survey of adults aged 18 to 44 the adjusted OR for stroke was 1.82 (1.08 to 3.10), and 2.45 (1.31 to 4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month (Parekh et al., 2020; both as relayed by Page et al., 2020). A health-record database found a 3-year incidence of heart attack of 1.37% against 0.54% (RR 2.53, 2.45 to 2.61), an inpatient database found heart-attack admissions of young adults of 0.23% against 0.14% among people using cannabis without other substances, and a systematic review of studies and case reports found that 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of both acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (all as relayed by Page et al., 2020). Laboratory studies show dose-related rises in heart rate and angina brought on by smoking cannabis in people with heart disease, exercise time to angina falling by 48% against placebo in one. Hall (2015) reads the evidence as consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults, adds a French series of cannabis-related hospitalisations that included heart attacks and a fatal stroke in young adults with no other known risk factors, and concludes that cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of heart attack; Volkow et al. (2014) describe use as associated with vascular conditions that raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication.
set.debate.evidence_no: In the CARDIA cohort, 5,113 adults aged 18 to 30 at the 1985–1986 baseline and followed for more than 25 years, cumulative lifetime and recent use were not associated with new cardiovascular disease, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, coronary heart disease or cardiac death (Reis et al., as relayed by Page et al., 2020), and in the same cohort higher aortic and coronary calcium went with cannabis only in people who had ever smoked tobacco (Auer et al., 3,498 participants). After a heart attack, long-term mortality was 29% higher in people who used cannabis but not significantly (95% CI 0.81 to 2.05; 3,886 patients; Frost et al.), and in hospital records of more than 1.2 million heart-attack patients a composite outcome (death, balloon pump, ventilation, cardiac arrest or shock) was not associated with cannabis use and mortality was lower (OR 0.79, no interval; short-term outcomes by the reference title; Johnson-Sasso et al.). The AHA statement warns that studies restricted to hospitalised patients carry a high probability of selection bias, so cannabis as a cause of hospitalisation is uncertain; that most data are short-term, observational and retrospective, with poorly determined exposure, recall bias and low-risk cohorts; and that tobacco and other drug use are inadequately handled in data collection and adjustment; citing a review of cannabis arteritis, it gives 97% as the share of people who smoke cannabis who also smoke tobacco. The 4.8-fold trigger estimate has no printed interval and rests on few exposed people, the 4.7 estimate for weekly use has no stated adjustment, the higher mortality after a heart attack in young adults is given for cocaine and marijuana use together, and the database estimates are crude or silent on adjustment (Page et al., 2020). The AHA writing group judges the evidence still inconclusive overall and insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors.
set.debate.neither_can_show: Whether cannabis itself causes any of these events: none of the relayed studies convincingly separates cannabis from tobacco, which most people who smoke cannabis also use, or from other drugs, and none is a sibling comparison or a genetically informed design. The case-crossover design removes stable differences between people, but it concerns the minutes to hours after use and rests on few exposed people and on their recall of timing, while CARDIA concerns decades of use in young adults with few events, so the two results need not conflict. Whether results from smoked cannabis apply to eating or vaping it, and whether older studies apply to today's stronger products, which the statement itself questions. How large any risk is for a given person: no source gives absolute rates by age and baseline risk. All figures here are second-hand, and several rows of the statement's own table cannot be right as printed (card sc_page_2020).
set.debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From second-hand sources only: the clearest signal is short-lived, a higher chance of a heart attack starting in the hour after use, from one case-crossover study with few exposed people, together with laboratory evidence that cannabis raises heart rate and can bring on angina in people with heart disease. Signals for stroke come from two surveys and lie mainly in frequent use; the hospital-database associations are hard to read because of selection bias, unstated adjustment and tobacco. The one long cohort of young adults found no association with new heart disease or stroke over 25 years, which fits a short-lived trigger as well as no effect, because such a cohort has few events. After a heart attack the relayed findings run both ways, and the one higher-mortality estimate does not separate cannabis from cocaine. The AHA judges the evidence inconclusive and, for people with cardiac risk factors, insufficient, and the editors agree that no long-term risk figure can be given from these sources. The primary studies themselves have not been read for this page.
